lessons.title: How React renders
lessons.summary: Render, commit, reconciliation and keys: what actually makes a component update.
lessons.body:
## Two phases
A React update has a **render phase** and a **commit phase**.

- **Render** calls your component functions and builds a tree of elements (plain objects). It must be pure: same props and state in, same JSX out, no side effects. React may call it more than once (StrictMode does this deliberately in development) or throw the result away.
- **Commit** applies the minimum DOM changes, then runs layout effects and, after paint, effects.

## What triggers a render
A component re-renders when its **state changes**, when its **parent re-renders** (even if the props are identical, unless it is memoised), or when a **context** it reads changes. Props changing is not the trigger by itself: a parent render is.

## Reconciliation and keys
React compares the new element tree with the previous one level by level. Same type at the same position means keep the instance and update it; a different type means unmount and remount.

For lists, `key` tells React which item is which across renders.

```tsx
{todos.map((t) => <Row key={t.id} todo={t} />)}
```

Use a stable, unique id. An array index as key breaks when items are inserted, removed or reordered: state such as an input's text sticks to the wrong row. Changing a component's `key` on purpose is also the cleanest way to reset its state.

## Batching
State updates inside event handlers, timeouts and promises are **batched** into one render. `setCount(count + 1)` twice still adds one because both read the same stale `count`; `setCount((c) => c + 1)` twice adds two.

## State is a snapshot
Each render sees its own constants. A handler created in render N always sees the state of render N, which is why closures can look "stale" in effects and timers.
keyPoints: Render must be pure; side effects belong in handlers and effects
A parent render re-renders children unless they are memoised
Keys identify list items across renders: stable ids, not indexes
Updates are batched; use the functional form when the next value depends on the previous
Changing `key` resets a component's state

lessons.title: Hooks and effects without the bugs
lessons.summary: The rules of hooks, closures, dependency arrays and why most effects shouldn't exist.
lessons.body:
## Rules of hooks
Call hooks only at the top level of a component or custom hook, never in conditions, loops or after an early return. React matches hooks to state by **call order**, so the order must be identical every render.

## The core hooks
- `useState`: local state. Updating schedules a re-render with the new snapshot.
- `useRef`: a mutable box that survives renders and does **not** trigger one. Use it for DOM nodes, timers, "latest value" holders.
- `useMemo` / `useCallback`: cache a value or function between renders when dependencies are unchanged. They are optimisations, not guarantees.
- `useReducer`: state transitions in one pure function; good for related fields.

## Effects synchronise with the outside world
`useEffect` runs **after paint** to synchronise something external (a subscription, a network connection, a non-React widget) with your state. The dependency array lists every reactive value the effect reads. Return a cleanup function; it runs before the next effect and on unmount.

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  const ws = new WebSocket(`/rooms/${roomId}`);
  ws.onmessage = (e) => setMessages((m) => [...m, e.data]);
  return () => ws.close();       // cleanup on roomId change or unmount
}, [roomId]);
```

## Stale closures
An effect or callback captures the values from the render it was created in. If it reads `count` but you omit it from the deps, it keeps seeing the old one. Fix it by listing the dependency, using the functional setter, or keeping the latest value in a ref.

## You might not need an effect
Do not use an effect to derive data from props or state (compute it during render), to respond to a click (use the handler), or to reset state when a prop changes (use a `key`). Fetching in an effect also needs cancel/ignore logic for races, which is why data libraries or framework loaders are preferred.
keyPoints: Hooks are matched by call order: never call them conditionally
Effects synchronise with external systems and need cleanup
The dependency array must list every reactive value the effect uses
Derive values during render; events belong in handlers
Refs hold mutable values without re-rendering

lessons.title: State architecture
lessons.summary: Where state should live: local, lifted, context, reducers, and server state libraries.
lessons.body:
## Put state as low as it can go
Keep state in the component that uses it. **Lift it** to the nearest common parent only when two siblings need it. Moving state up widens the re-render area, so do it deliberately.

## Derived state is not state
If you can compute it from other state or props, compute it. Storing both a list and its filtered copy invites them to drift apart.

## Context is for slowly changing, widely read values
Theme, current user, locale. A context value change re-renders **every** consumer, so a frequently changing value (mouse position, a large store) in one context is a performance trap. Split contexts, memoise the value object, or use a store with selectors.

## Reducers for related transitions
When several fields change together or the next state depends on an action, `useReducer` makes transitions explicit and testable as a pure function.

## Server state is a different thing
Data that lives on a server (users, posts) is **cached, shared and can go stale**. Treat it with a tool built for that (TanStack Query, SWR, or framework loaders): caching, deduplication, background refetch, retries, invalidation after mutations, optimistic updates. Keeping it in `useState` + `useEffect` reimplements all of that, usually with races.

## Client stores
For genuinely global client state (a drawing canvas, a multi-step wizard) a small store such as Zustand, with selector subscriptions, avoids the context re-render problem.

## Forms
Prefer uncontrolled inputs or a form library for large forms; controlled inputs re-render on every keystroke.

## Rule of thumb
URL for shareable state (filters, tabs, page), server-state library for remote data, local state for UI, context for app-wide constants, a store only when you can name why the others fail.
keyPoints: Keep state close to where it is used; lift only when needed
Compute derived values instead of storing them
Context changes re-render all consumers: use it for slow-moving values
Server state needs caching and invalidation, so use a purpose-built library

lessons.title: React performance
lessons.summary: Measure first: memoisation, transitions, virtualisation, splitting, and the compiler.
lessons.body:
## Measure before optimising
Use the React DevTools Profiler to see what rendered and why, and the browser Performance panel for long tasks. Most apps have two or three real hotspots; the rest of the code does not need memoisation.

## Reduce the work
- **Move state down** or split a component so the frequently changing part is small.
- **Pass children as props**: a wrapper holding fast-changing state can render `{children}` that were created by a parent and so don't re-render.
- **`React.memo`** skips re-rendering a component when props are shallow-equal. It only helps when the props are stable, so pair it with `useMemo`/`useCallback` for object and function props, or let the **React Compiler** insert that memoisation automatically.

## Keep input responsive
`useTransition` and `useDeferredValue` mark an update as non-urgent so typing stays smooth while a heavy list re-renders in the background.

## Long lists
Rendering thousands of rows is slow regardless of memoisation. **Virtualise** (TanStack Virtual, react-window): only the visible rows exist in the DOM.

## Ship less JavaScript
Code-split routes and heavy widgets with `lazy` / dynamic `import()`, avoid importing whole libraries for one function, and prefer Server Components where available so that code never reaches the client.

## Avoid layout thrash and big images
Animate `transform` and `opacity`, size images, and avoid reading layout in a loop.

Smaller components and moved-down state beat memo everywhere

lessons.title: Next.js App Router model
lessons.summary: Server and Client Components, layouts, streaming, and the async request APIs.
lessons.body:
## Server Components by default
In the App Router every component is a **Server Component** unless a file starts with `"use client"`. Server Components run only on the server: they can read the database, use secrets, and ship **no JavaScript** to the browser. Client Components are for interactivity (state, effects, event handlers, browser APIs).

The boundary rule: a Server Component can import and render Client Components, and can pass them serialisable props (and Server Components as `children`). A Client Component cannot import a Server Component, because it would have to ship its code.

## File conventions
- `layout.tsx` wraps its segment and **persists across navigation** (state is kept, it doesn't re-render).
- `page.tsx` makes the route public.
- `loading.tsx` is an instant Suspense fallback; `error.tsx` is an error boundary; `not-found.tsx` handles `notFound()`.
- Route handlers (`route.ts`) are API endpoints.

## Streaming
A page can send its shell immediately and **stream** slower parts as they resolve, by wrapping them in `<Suspense>`. Users see content progressively instead of waiting for the slowest query.

## Async request APIs
In current versions `cookies()`, `headers()`, `params` and `searchParams` are **async**: `const { id } = await params`. Reading them makes a route dynamic (rendered per request).

## Server Actions
A function marked `"use server"` that a form or client call invokes as an RPC. Treat each one as a public endpoint: **authenticate and validate input inside it**, because the client can call it with anything.

## Common mistakes
Putting `"use client"` at the top of a layout (it pulls the whole subtree to the client), passing non-serialisable props across the boundary, and fetching in a Client Component what a Server Component could read directly.

lessons.title: Data fetching and caching
lessons.summary: Static vs dynamic rendering, revalidation, and where the caches are.
lessons.body:
## Fetch on the server
Server Components can be `async` and await data directly. Fetch in parallel with `Promise.all` instead of awaiting one request after another (a **waterfall**), and use Suspense so a slow request does not block the page.

## Static vs dynamic
A route is **static** when everything it needs is known at build time (or cached), and **dynamic** when it reads per-request data such as cookies, headers or search params. Static output is served from a CDN: fastest and cheapest. Choose dynamic only where the data is personal or must be fresh.

## Caching layers (the part people confuse)
1. **Request memoisation**: identical `fetch` calls (or functions wrapped in `cache`) during one render are de-duplicated.
2. **Data cache**: results persisted across requests, controlled by revalidation.
3. **Full route / CDN cache**: the rendered output of a static route.
4. **Client router cache**: pages already visited are kept in the browser for quick back/forward.

Defaults have changed between Next.js versions, so read the version-specific guide rather than relying on memory. Recent versions move toward explicit opt-in caching (`"use cache"` with cache lifetimes and tags).

## Revalidation
- **Time based**: serve a cached result and refresh it after N seconds (stale-while-revalidate).
- **On demand**: after a mutation, invalidate by **path** or **tag** (`revalidatePath`, `revalidateTag`) so the next request is fresh.

## Mutations
Use Server Actions for writes, then revalidate what the write affected. Forgetting to invalidate is the classic "I saved but the page still shows old data" bug.

## Choosing
Public, rarely changing: static with time or tag revalidation. Personalised: dynamic, with cacheable sub-parts streamed in. Highly interactive: client-side library for the live parts.

Static is served from the CDN; dynamic reads per-request data

lessons.title: Auth and security in Next.js
lessons.summary: Sessions, cookies, where to check authorisation, and Server Action safety.
lessons.body:
## Sessions vs JWT
A **session cookie** holds an opaque id (or a signed, encrypted payload) and the server looks up the rest; it can be revoked instantly. A **JWT** is self-contained and verifiable without a lookup but hard to revoke before it expires. For a single web app, a signed `httpOnly` session cookie is usually the simplest and safest choice.

## Cookie flags
`HttpOnly` (JavaScript can't read it, limits XSS damage), `Secure` (HTTPS only), `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict` (blocks most CSRF), a sensible `Max-Age`, and a `__Host-` prefix where possible.

## Where to check authorisation
**Check next to the data**, not only at the edge. A proxy/middleware redirect is a convenience, not a security boundary: a request can reach a Server Action or route handler directly. Every Server Action, route handler and data-access function must verify the session and the user's right to that record. Putting the check in a data-access layer makes it hard to forget.

## Validate everything
Server Action arguments and route handler bodies are untrusted. Parse them with a schema validator (zod) and return typed errors. Never build SQL or Mongo queries by string concatenation; use parameters and reject operator objects in Mongo filters.

## CSRF
Server Actions compare the `Origin` header to the host and are POST-only, which covers most CSRF. For custom route handlers that mutate state, check origin or use tokens, and keep cookies `SameSite`.

## XSS and headers
React escapes output; the danger is `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, user-controlled `href` (`javascript:`), and untrusted markdown. Set a Content-Security-Policy, `X-Content-Type-Options`, and `frame-ancestors`.

## Secrets
Only `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variables reach the browser. Keep every key server-side and never log tokens.

Authorise next to the data, not only in middleware/proxy
Treat every Server Action and route handler as a public endpoint
Validate input with a schema; parameterise queries

lessons.title: Rendering strategies and web performance
lessons.summary: SSR, SSG, ISR, partial prerendering and the Core Web Vitals that users feel.
lessons.body:
## Strategies
- **SSG** (static): HTML built once at build time. Fastest, great for docs and marketing.
- **SSR** (dynamic): HTML built per request. For personalised or always-fresh pages.
- **ISR**: static HTML refreshed in the background after a time or an event.
- **Partial prerendering**: a static shell served instantly with dynamic holes streamed in.
- **CSR**: render in the browser; use for highly interactive widgets behind login.

## Core Web Vitals
- **LCP** (Largest Contentful Paint): how fast the main content appears. Target under about 2.5 s. Improve with server rendering, a small critical path, preloading the hero image, and a CDN.
- **INP** (Interaction to Next Paint): how quickly the page responds to input. Target under about 200 ms. Reduce long tasks, ship less JS, use transitions.
- **CLS** (Cumulative Layout Shift): visual stability. Target under about 0.1. Always set image dimensions and reserve space for late content.

## Practical levers
`next/image` for responsive, lazy-loaded, correctly sized images; `next/font` to avoid layout shift and extra requests; dynamic `import()` for heavy client code; prefetching of visible links (the router does it); keep third-party scripts off the critical path.

## Measure with real data
Lab tools (Lighthouse) find problems; **field data** (real-user monitoring, CrUX) tells you what users actually experience. Budget bundle size per route and watch it in CI.

lessons.title: Designing a Node.js API
lessons.summary: Layering, validation, error handling, pagination and idempotency for a production REST API.
lessons.body:
## Layers keep code testable
Split a request path into **controller/route** (HTTP in and out), **service** (business rules, no HTTP types), and **repository** (the only code that knows the database). The service can then be unit tested with a fake repository, and swapping Postgres for Mongo touches one layer.

## Validate at the edge
Parse `body`, `query` and `params` with a schema (zod, class-validator) before they reach a service. Reject unknown fields, coerce types, and return **400 with field-level errors**. Never trust `req.body`.

## One error model
Throw typed errors (`NotFound`, `Conflict`, `Forbidden`) in services and translate them in **one** error handler to status codes and a stable JSON shape (`{ error: { code, message, details } }`). Don't leak stack traces or SQL errors.

## Pagination
Offset pagination (`?page=3&limit=20`) is simple but slow on deep pages and unstable when rows are inserted. **Cursor pagination** (`?after=<last id>`) uses an indexed seek (`WHERE id > $1 ORDER BY id LIMIT 20`) and stays fast and consistent. Always cap `limit`.

## Idempotency
Networks retry. `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE` are idempotent by definition; `POST` is not. For payments and order creation accept an **`Idempotency-Key`** header, store the key with the result, and return the stored result on a repeat.

## Concurrency control
Prevent lost updates with **optimistic locking**: add a `version` column, update `WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2`, and return 409 if no row changed.

## Operational basics
Structured JSON logs with a request id, graceful shutdown (stop accepting, drain, close pools), health and readiness endpoints, timeouts on every outbound call, and configuration from the environment.

lessons.title: NestJS core: modules, providers and DI
lessons.summary: How Nest organises an app and how dependency injection actually works.
lessons.body:
## What Nest adds
NestJS is an opinionated framework on top of Express (or Fastify) that gives a Node API a **structure**: modules, controllers, providers, and a dependency-injection container. It resembles Angular's architecture.

## The building blocks
- **Module** (`@Module`): a cohesive feature boundary. It declares `controllers`, `providers`, `imports` (other modules) and `exports` (providers others may use).
- **Controller** (`@Controller`): maps HTTP routes to handler methods; it should be thin.
- **Provider** (`@Injectable`): anything injectable, usually a service with business logic or a repository.

```ts
@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(private readonly repo: OrdersRepository, private readonly events: EventBus) {}
}

@Module({ imports: [DatabaseModule], providers: [OrdersService, OrdersRepository], controllers: [OrdersController], exports: [OrdersService] })
export class OrdersModule {}
```

## Dependency injection
Nest reads the constructor parameter **types** (through decorator metadata) and resolves each from the container, building a graph and instantiating providers once. You write classes against abstractions and let the container wire them, so tests can substitute a fake provider.

- **Scopes**: providers are **singletons** by default. `REQUEST` scope creates one per request (it propagates up the dependency chain and costs performance), `TRANSIENT` creates one per injection.
- **Custom providers**: `useClass`, `useValue`, `useFactory` (with `inject`), and string/symbol tokens for interfaces, since interfaces don't exist at runtime.
- **Dynamic modules**: `ConfigModule.forRoot()` style modules that take configuration.

## Boundaries that scale
A module should expose a small public surface via `exports`. Importing another feature's repository directly couples modules; export a service instead. **Circular dependencies** between modules or providers signal a design problem (extract a third module, or use `forwardRef` as a last resort).

Controllers stay thin; providers hold logic

lessons.title: NestJS request pipeline
lessons.summary: Middleware, guards, interceptors, pipes and filters: what runs when and what each is for.
lessons.body:
## The order
For an incoming request Nest runs, in order:

1. **Middleware** (Express-style, before routing)
2. **Guards** (can this request proceed?)
3. **Interceptors** (before the handler)
4. **Pipes** (transform and validate arguments)
5. **Handler** (your controller method)
6. **Interceptors** (after, on the response)
7. **Exception filters** (if anything threw)

## What each is for
- **Guard**: authentication and authorisation. Implements `canActivate(context)` and returns true or false (or throws). Because it has the execution context, it can read route metadata set by decorators such as `@Roles('admin')` through `Reflector`.
- **Pipe**: validation and transformation of a single argument. `ValidationPipe` with class-validator DTOs rejects bad bodies with 400; `ParseIntPipe` converts a param. With `whitelist: true` unknown properties are stripped, with `forbidNonWhitelisted` they are rejected.
- **Interceptor**: cross-cutting logic around the handler using RxJS: logging with timing, response mapping, caching, timeouts, retries.
- **Exception filter**: turns exceptions into responses; a global filter gives one consistent error shape.
- **Middleware**: low-level request work (request ids, raw body, CORS), not business rules.

## Binding scope
Apply any of them at three levels: **global** (`app.useGlobalPipes`), **controller**, or **method**. Prefer global for validation and error filtering so nothing is forgotten, and use `APP_GUARD`/`APP_PIPE` providers when they need DI.

## DTOs
Define input shapes as classes with validation decorators (or generate them from zod). Never use the database entity as the request type: it exposes fields clients must not set (like `role`).

## Example guard
```ts
@Injectable()
export class SessionGuard implements CanActivate {
  constructor(private readonly auth: AuthService) {}
  async canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext) {
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest();
    req.user = await this.auth.verify(req.cookies?.session);
    return Boolean(req.user);
  }
}
```

lessons.title: NestJS testing, queues and scale
lessons.summary: Testing modules, background jobs, microservice transports, and modular monolith first.
lessons.body:
## Testing
- **Unit tests** build a testing module that provides the class under test with **fake providers**: `Test.createTestingModule({ providers: [OrdersService, { provide: OrdersRepository, useValue: fakeRepo }] })`. Nothing else starts.
- **Integration / e2e tests** boot the real app (or a slice) and use **supertest** against a test database (a container or in-memory instance), asserting HTTP behaviour including guards and validation.
- Override a real provider for one test with `.overrideProvider(X).useValue(fake)`.

## Configuration
`@nestjs/config` loads and validates environment variables at startup (fail fast on a missing secret). Inject `ConfigService` rather than reading `process.env` everywhere.

## Background work
Do not make users wait for slow work. Put it on a **queue** (BullMQ on Redis is the common Nest choice): the request enqueues a job and returns; a worker process consumes it with retries, backoff and a dead-letter state. Make jobs **idempotent** because they can run more than once.

## Events and scheduling
`@nestjs/event-emitter` for in-process domain events, `@nestjs/schedule` for cron jobs (remember that with several instances a cron fires on each one: use a lock or a single scheduler).

## Microservices
Nest supports transports such as TCP, Redis, NATS, Kafka and gRPC with `@MessagePattern`. Start with a **modular monolith** (clear module boundaries, one deployable). Split out a service only for a concrete reason: independent scaling, a different team, different reliability needs. Distributed systems add network failure, versioning and observability costs.

## Performance
Use the Fastify adapter if raw throughput matters, enable compression and caching deliberately, keep request-scoped providers rare, and measure before tuning.

lessons.title: Reading query plans
lessons.summary: EXPLAIN ANALYZE, scan types, join algorithms and why statistics matter.
lessons.body:
## Always look at the plan
The planner chooses how to execute SQL. `EXPLAIN` shows its estimate, and `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` runs the query and shows what actually happened, including real row counts, time, and buffer hits. Compare **estimated rows vs actual rows**: a big gap means bad statistics and usually a bad plan.

## Scan types (PostgreSQL names)
- **Seq Scan**: read the whole table. Fine for small tables or when most rows are needed.
- **Index Scan**: walk an index and fetch matching heap rows.
- **Index Only Scan**: answer from the index alone (needs the visibility map to be current).
- **Bitmap Index/Heap Scan**: combine several index conditions, then read pages in physical order.

## Join algorithms
- **Nested loop**: for each outer row, probe the inner side. Excellent when the outer set is small and the inner has an index.
- **Hash join**: build a hash table of the smaller input, probe with the larger. Good for large unsorted equi-joins.
- **Merge join**: both inputs sorted on the key; good when already ordered by an index.

## What slows queries
- Functions on indexed columns (`WHERE lower(email) = ...` can't use a plain index; use an expression index).
- Leading wildcards (`LIKE '%abc'`).
- Implicit casts that defeat an index (`WHERE varchar_col = 123`).
- `SELECT *` pulling wide rows, and `OFFSET` on deep pages.
- N+1 queries from an ORM: one query per row instead of a join or `IN` batch.

## Statistics
`ANALYZE` refreshes the table statistics the planner uses. Autovacuum normally does it; after a large bulk load run it yourself. Correlated columns can fool the planner: extended statistics (`CREATE STATISTICS`) can help.

## Method
Find the slow query (pg_stat_statements), get the real plan, locate the node with the biggest actual time, check estimates vs actuals, then fix with an index, a rewrite, or fresh statistics. Re-measure.

lessons.title: Indexing that works
lessons.summary: B-tree rules, composite order, covering and partial indexes, and the cost of writes.
lessons.body:
## What an index is
A B-tree index is a sorted structure over one or more columns that lets the database find rows by key in O(log n) and read ranges in order, without scanning the table. Primary keys and unique constraints create one automatically.

## Composite index order
For an index on `(a, b, c)`, the database can use a **left prefix**: `a`; `a, b`; `a, b, c`. It can't efficiently use `b` alone. Put **equality** columns first, then the **range or sort** column. For `WHERE tenant_id = ? AND created_at > ? ORDER BY created_at`, the index `(tenant_id, created_at)` serves the filter and the sort.

## Selectivity
An index on a column with few distinct values (a boolean) rarely helps by itself, because the planner would read most of the table anyway. Combine low-selectivity columns with selective ones, or use a **partial index** that covers only the interesting rows: `CREATE INDEX ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending';`.

## Covering indexes
`INCLUDE (cols)` adds non-key columns to the index so a query is answered from the index alone (an index-only scan), skipping the table fetch.

## Other index types
- **GIN** for arrays, JSONB containment and full-text search.
- **GiST/SP-GiST** for geometry and ranges.
- **BRIN** for huge append-mostly tables ordered by time: tiny and cheap.
- **Hash** for pure equality (rarely needed).

## The cost
Every index slows writes (each insert/update must maintain it), uses disk and memory, and can be bypassed by bad queries. Add indexes for real, measured query patterns; drop unused ones (`pg_stat_user_indexes`). Create indexes on live tables with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`.

## Foreign keys
Postgres does not index foreign key columns automatically. Index them or joins and cascading deletes become slow.

lessons.title: Transactions, isolation and locking
lessons.summary: ACID in practice, MVCC, isolation levels, deadlocks and safe concurrent updates.
lessons.body:
## ACID in one line each
**Atomicity** all or nothing. **Consistency** constraints hold. **Isolation** concurrent transactions don't see each other's partial work. **Durability** committed data survives a crash (the write-ahead log).

## MVCC
PostgreSQL (and most modern engines) keep **multiple versions** of a row. Readers see a consistent snapshot and don't block writers; writers don't block readers. Old versions are cleaned by VACUUM, so long-running transactions cause bloat.

## Isolation levels and anomalies
| Level | Dirty read | Non-repeatable read | Phantom | Write skew |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Read committed (Postgres default) | no | possible | possible | possible |
| Repeatable read (snapshot) | no | no | no in Postgres | possible |
| Serializable | no | no | no | no (may abort) |

Higher isolation means more aborts to retry. **Serializable** transactions can fail with a serialization error: your code must **retry** the transaction.

## Lost update and the fixes
Two transactions read a balance, both add 10, both write: one update is lost. Solutions:
1. Do the arithmetic in SQL: `UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + 10 WHERE id = 1` (atomic).
2. Lock the row: `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`.
3. Optimistic version check with retry.
4. Serializable isolation with retry.

## Locking tools
`FOR UPDATE` locks selected rows; `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` lets many workers pull different jobs from a queue table without blocking each other; advisory locks give app-level mutexes.

## Deadlocks
Two transactions each hold a lock the other wants. The database detects it and aborts one. Prevent by **locking rows in a consistent order**, keeping transactions short, and never waiting on a user or a network call while holding locks.

## Practice
Keep transactions small, set statement and lock timeouts, and handle serialization and deadlock errors with a bounded retry loop.

lessons.title: Schema design and safe migrations
lessons.summary: Modelling choices, constraints, zero-downtime migrations and connection pooling.
lessons.body:
## Model with constraints
Let the database enforce truth: `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`, `CHECK`, foreign keys with a deliberate `ON DELETE` rule. Application checks alone race under concurrency; a unique constraint cannot.

## Keys
- **Surrogate keys** (bigint identity or UUID) don't change and join fast. Use a natural unique constraint alongside.
- **UUIDv4** keys scatter inserts across the index (poor locality, bigger); **UUIDv7 / ULID** are time-ordered and keep inserts sequential. In a distributed SQL database, random keys avoid hot spots, so the trade-off flips.

## Normalise first, denormalise on evidence
Third normal form avoids update anomalies. Denormalise (a counter, a copied name, a materialised view) only when a measured read path needs it, and keep it correct with constraints or a single writer.

## Types
Money in integer minor units or `numeric`, never float. Store timestamps as `timestamptz` in UTC. Use `jsonb` for genuinely flexible attributes, not as a way to avoid modelling.

## Zero-downtime migrations: expand and contract
1. **Expand**: add the new column/table as nullable or with a default (careful: some defaults rewrite the table on older versions).
2. **Deploy** code that writes both and reads the old one; **backfill** in small batches.
3. Switch reads to the new column.
4. **Contract**: drop the old column in a later release.

Dangerous on large tables: adding a column with a volatile default, creating an index without `CONCURRENTLY`, adding `NOT NULL` or a foreign key without first validating (`NOT VALID` then `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT`), and long `ALTER` statements that wait for a lock and block every query behind them. Set a `lock_timeout` for migrations.

## Connection pooling
Each Postgres connection is a process with real memory, so thousands of app connections fall over. Use a pool in the app and **PgBouncer** between app and database (transaction pooling). Serverless functions especially need a pooler, because each cold instance opens its own connections.

Time-ordered ids keep B-tree inserts local; random ids suit distributed SQL

lessons.title: MongoDB data modelling
lessons.summary: Embed vs reference, the patterns that matter, and schema validation.
lessons.body:
## Model for your queries
MongoDB stores JSON-like documents (BSON) up to 16 MB. The central rule is: **model data the way your application reads it**. Documents that are read together should usually live together, so one read replaces a join.

## Embed or reference?
**Embed** when the child data is read with the parent, belongs to one parent, is bounded in size and changes together. Examples: an order's line items, a user's addresses.

**Reference** (store the child's `_id`) when the child is shared by many parents, grows without bound, or is updated independently. Examples: a post's comments (unbounded), a product referenced by many orders.

Use `$lookup` for occasional joins, but if every query needs one, you probably should have embedded or denormalised.

## Useful patterns
- **Subset pattern**: keep the 10 most recent or most relevant children embedded and the rest in another collection.
- **Bucket pattern**: group time-series or IoT readings into one document per hour or device to cut document count and index size (or use native time-series collections).
- **Computed pattern**: store a pre-computed counter or total updated on write, to avoid expensive aggregation on read.
- **Extended reference**: copy a few frequently displayed fields (a customer's name) into the referencing document, accepting that you must update copies.
- **Outlier pattern**: handle the one celebrity with 5 million followers differently from the average user.

## Anti-patterns
Unbounded arrays that grow forever (documents hit the size limit and every write rewrites a huge document), too many collections or indexes, massive documents read for one field, and treating Mongo as a relational database with a collection per table.

## Schema validation
Flexible schema does not mean no schema. Use `$jsonSchema` validators on the collection (or Mongoose schemas in the app), validate with `validationLevel`/`validationAction`, and plan **schema versioning**: add a `schemaVersion` field and migrate lazily or in batches.

## Atomicity
A single-document write is **atomic**, including nested fields and arrays. Embedding related data therefore gives you atomic updates without a multi-document transaction.

lessons.title: Indexes and the aggregation pipeline
lessons.summary: Compound index design (the ESR rule), explain, and how pipelines run.
lessons.body:
## Indexes
Without an index MongoDB does a **collection scan**. Indexes are B-trees; `_id` is always indexed. Create them for your real queries and confirm with `explain("executionStats")`: look for `IXSCAN` rather than `COLLSCAN`, and compare `totalDocsExamined` and `totalKeysExamined` with `nReturned`. A well-indexed query examines roughly as many keys as it returns.

## Compound indexes and the ESR rule
Order index fields as **Equality, Sort, Range**:

```js
// query: status = 'open', sort by createdAt desc, amount > 100
db.orders.createIndex({ status: 1, createdAt: -1, amount: 1 })
```

Equality fields narrow first, the sort field then comes out already ordered (avoiding an in-memory sort, which has a memory limit), and range fields last. Like SQL, an index serves a **prefix** of its fields.

## Index types and options
Single field, compound, multikey (arrays), text, geospatial (2dsphere), hashed (for hashed sharding), **TTL** (expire documents after a time), **partial** (index only matching documents), **unique**, and **sparse**. A **covered query** is answered from the index alone when the filter and projection use only indexed fields.

## Aggregation pipeline
A pipeline is a sequence of stages, each transforming the stream of documents:

```js
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: 'paid', createdAt: { $gte: since } } }, // filter early, uses index
  { $group: { _id: '$customerId', total: { $sum: '$amount' } } },
  { $sort: { total: -1 } },
  { $limit: 10 },
  { $lookup: { from: 'customers', localField: '_id', foreignField: '_id', as: 'customer' } }
])
```

Put `$match` and `$sort` that can use an index **first**, and reduce data (`$project`, `$limit`) before expensive stages. `$group` and `$sort` have a memory limit per stage unless `allowDiskUse` is set. For repeated heavy reports, precompute with `$merge` into a summary collection.

## Practice
Keep the working set (hot data and indexes) in RAM, avoid regexes that can't use an index (unanchored or case-insensitive without a collation index), and remove unused indexes (`$indexStats`).

lessons.title: Replication and sharding
lessons.summary: Replica sets, elections, read and write concerns, shard keys and hot shards.
lessons.body:
## Replica sets
A **replica set** is a group of `mongod` nodes holding the same data: one **primary** takes writes, **secondaries** replicate its **oplog** asynchronously. If the primary fails, the remaining voting members hold an **election** (Raft-like) and a secondary becomes primary, typically within seconds. Use an odd number of voting members (3 or 5) so a majority exists. The driver reconnects automatically; make writes **retryable**.

## Write concern, read concern, read preference
- **Write concern** says how many members must acknowledge: `w: 1` (primary only), `w: "majority"` (survives failover, the sensible default for important data), and `j: true` for the journal.
- **Read concern** controls what you may read: `local`, `majority` (only majority-committed data, so it can't be rolled back), `linearizable`, `snapshot` (in transactions).
- **Read preference** chooses where to read: `primary` (default), `secondary` (scales reads but can be stale), `nearest`.

`w:1` with a primary failure can **lose** acknowledged writes that had not replicated (they roll back); `w:"majority"` cannot.

## Sharding
Sharding splits a collection across **shards** (each a replica set) to scale storage and throughput horizontally. `mongos` routers send requests to the right shard using config server metadata. Data is split into **chunks** by the **shard key**; a balancer moves chunks between shards.

## Choosing the shard key (the decision you can't easily undo)
A good key has **high cardinality**, **even distribution** of writes, and appears in most queries (so they target one shard rather than scatter-gather).

- **Ranged** on a monotonically increasing key (timestamp, ObjectId) sends all inserts to the **last chunk**: a **hot shard**.
- **Hashed** keys spread writes evenly but turn range queries into scatter-gather.
- **Compound keys** such as `{ tenantId: 1, _id: 1 }` keep one tenant's data together while distributing tenants.
- Resharding is possible in recent versions but expensive: choose carefully.

## When to shard
Not early. Scale up, index well and use replicas first. Shard when data or write throughput exceeds one replica set, or for data-locality requirements (zone sharding).

lessons.title: Distributed database fundamentals
lessons.summary: CAP and PACELC, replication, partitioning, quorums and consensus.
lessons.body:
## Why distribute
One machine limits storage, throughput and availability. Distributing data gives **scale** (partitioning), **availability** (replication) and **latency** (data near users), at the cost of network failures, partial failure and clock problems.

## CAP, stated carefully
During a network **partition** you must choose: **consistency** (every read sees the latest write or an error) or **availability** (every request gets a non-error answer, maybe stale). Partitions happen, so the real choice is C or A **when one occurs**. **PACELC** adds the everyday trade-off: *else* (no partition) you still choose between **latency** and **consistency**.

## Replication
- **Single leader**: one node accepts writes and streams a log to followers. Simple; the leader is a bottleneck, failover is delicate.
- **Multi-leader**: several accept writes, needing conflict resolution. Useful for multi-region and offline clients.
- **Leaderless** (Dynamo-style: Cassandra, DynamoDB internals): any replica accepts reads and writes with **quorums**.

## Quorums
With `N` replicas, a write acknowledged by `W` and a read from `R`, if **R + W > N** the read set overlaps the latest write. N=3, W=2, R=2 tolerates one failure with strong-ish reads. Lower W or R trades consistency for latency.

## Partitioning (sharding)
Split data by **key range** (good for range scans, risk of hot spots) or **hash** (even spread, no range scans), or **consistent hashing** so adding a node moves only a fraction of keys. Secondary indexes are either local (scatter-gather reads) or global (slower writes).

## Consensus
To agree on a single value or an ordered log despite failures, systems use **Raft** or **Paxos**: elect a leader for a term, the leader appends entries, and an entry is **committed** once a **majority** stores it. With 2f+1 nodes you tolerate f failures. Consensus gives linearizable, fault-tolerant metadata and replicated state machines, at the cost of a round trip to a majority per write.

## Time
Wall clocks drift, so ordering across machines can't rely on them. Systems use logical clocks, **hybrid logical clocks (HLC)**, or bounded-uncertainty clocks (Google Spanner's TrueTime).

## Consistency models
From strongest: **linearizable**, **serializable** (for transactions), sequential, causal, **eventual**. Know which your database provides by default.

lessons.title: CockroachDB architecture
lessons.summary: A distributed SQL database: ranges, Raft, leaseholders, MVCC and serializable isolation.
lessons.body:
## What it is
CockroachDB is a **distributed SQL database** that speaks the PostgreSQL wire protocol, scales horizontally, survives node, zone and even region failures, and gives **serializable** transactions by default. It is built to be "NewSQL": SQL and ACID with a Spanner-like architecture.

## Layers
1. **SQL layer**: parses and plans SQL (Postgres-compatible, but not identical) and turns it into key-value operations.
2. **Transaction layer**: implements distributed ACID transactions across ranges.
3. **Distribution layer**: maps keys to ranges and nodes.
4. **Replication layer**: Raft per range.
5. **Storage layer**: a local key-value engine (Pebble) with **MVCC**.

## Ranges and Raft
The whole keyspace is split into contiguous **ranges** (about 512 MiB by default). Each range is replicated, normally **3 times**, and each range is its own **Raft group**. Writes go through the range's Raft leader and commit when a majority of replicas have them. Ranges split as they grow and are rebalanced across nodes automatically.

## Leaseholder
For each range one replica is the **leaseholder**. It serves reads (without a Raft round trip) and coordinates writes, so a read is cheap and a write costs one consensus round. The leaseholder is usually the Raft leader and can move toward where traffic comes from.

## Transactions and time
CockroachDB uses MVCC with **hybrid logical clocks**. The default isolation is **SERIALIZABLE**. When transactions conflict it may **abort one with error code `40001`** (a retryable serialization failure), so **client code must retry**. Long, contended transactions are the enemy. Newer versions also offer read committed for workloads that want fewer retries.

## Resilience
Survival goals: **zone** failure (default) or **region** failure. Raft handles node loss with automatic leader election; the cluster keeps working as long as a majority of each affected range's replicas survive.

## Operating notes
Run at least 3 nodes, use a load balancer or the driver's multiple hosts, watch the DB Console (hot ranges, contention, SQL activity), and use CockroachDB Cloud (including a free serverless tier) to practise without managing nodes.

lessons.title: Modelling and operating on CockroachDB
lessons.summary: Primary keys that avoid hot spots, retries, multi-region tables and Postgres differences.
lessons.body:
## Avoid hot spots
Keys are stored in sorted order, so a **monotonically increasing primary key** (a `SERIAL` or timestamp) sends every insert to the **last range**, which one node serves: a write hot spot. Prefer **UUID** keys (`gen_random_uuid()`), or a **hash-sharded index** for sequential keys that must remain indexed in order. This is the opposite of the advice for a single-node Postgres, where sequential keys are friendly to the B-tree.

## Transaction retries
Wrap transactions in a **retry loop** for SQLSTATE `40001`. Most drivers and ORMs have helpers. Make the transaction body idempotent (it may run several times), keep it short, and don't do external side effects (sending email) inside it.

```ts
async function withRetry<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>, max = 5): Promise<T> {
  for (let i = 0; ; i++) {
    try { return await fn(); }
    catch (e: any) { if (e.code !== '40001' || i >= max) throw e; await sleep(2 ** i * 20 + Math.random() * 20); }
  }
}
```

## Reduce contention
Avoid updating one popular row from many transactions (a global counter): shard the counter across several rows and sum, or batch. Use `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` carefully, keep transactions small, and prefer a single statement or CTE over many round trips.

## Multi-region
Declare regions on the database and choose a table locality:
- **REGIONAL BY TABLE**: whole table homed in one region (fast there).
- **REGIONAL BY ROW**: each row homed in the region of its `crdb_region` column, so users get local latency for their own data.
- **GLOBAL**: low-latency reads everywhere, slower writes, for small read-mostly reference tables.

Choose a survival goal (zone or region) and accept the latency of cross-region consensus for region survival. **Follower reads** (`AS OF SYSTEM TIME follower_read_timestamp()`) read slightly stale data from the nearest replica.

## Compatibility differences from Postgres
Mostly compatible, but check: some extensions and features differ or are missing, sequences behave differently, large `OFFSET` is expensive as everywhere, and online schema changes run as background jobs. Test your ORM and migrations against it early.

## Where it fits
Choose it for horizontally scalable relational data, strong consistency, multi-region requirements and high availability (payments, ledgers, inventory). A single Postgres is simpler and cheaper when one node is enough.

lessons.title: Choosing a database
lessons.summary: A decision framework across Postgres, MongoDB, CockroachDB, DynamoDB/Cassandra, Redis and more.
lessons.body:
## Start from the workload, not the brand
Ask: what are the **access patterns**, the **consistency** needs, the **scale** (data size and write rate), the **latency** targets, and the **team's** skills and operations budget? Then pick the simplest thing that fits.

## The common choices
| Need | Good fit | Why |
|---|---|---|
| General relational data, joins, transactions, one region | **PostgreSQL** | Mature, rich SQL, JSONB, extensions, huge ecosystem. The default answer |
| Flexible documents, nested data, fast iteration | **MongoDB** | Document model, replica sets, sharding, good tooling |
| Relational + horizontal scale + multi-region + strong consistency | **CockroachDB** (also Spanner, YugabyteDB, TiDB) | Distributed SQL with serializable transactions |
| Massive scale, simple key access, predictable latency | **DynamoDB** / **Cassandra** | Partition-key access, tunable consistency, no joins |
| Caching, sessions, queues, rate limits, leaderboards | **Redis** | In-memory data structures |
| Full-text search, log analytics | **Elasticsearch / OpenSearch** | Inverted indexes, relevance |
| Time series and metrics | **TimescaleDB, InfluxDB, ClickHouse** | Columnar/time-optimised storage |
| Analytics on big data | **ClickHouse, BigQuery, Snowflake** | Columnar, vectorised scans |
| Relationships (graphs) | **Neo4j** | Traversals |
| Similarity search for embeddings | **pgvector, dedicated vector DBs** | ANN indexes |

## Rules of thumb
- **Postgres first.** It handles far more scale and variety than people expect, and one database is easier to run than three.
- Add a specialised store when a measured need appears (cache, search, analytics), keeping the main database as the source of truth, and feed the others through events or change data capture.
- Pick a distributed database for a real requirement (multi-region writes, scale beyond one node, region-level survival), not for fashion.
- Don't choose Mongo to avoid thinking about schema, or Postgres JSONB to avoid modelling; both pay back later.
- Operations matter: managed services reduce the burden for small teams.

## How to answer in an interview
State requirements, name the access patterns, pick a primary store with reasons, say what you would add later and why, and name the trade-off you accept (consistency, cost, complexity, lock-in).

lessons.title: Monolith, modular monolith, microservices
lessons.summary: How to split a system: boundaries first, services only when justified.
lessons.body:
## The spectrum
A **monolith** is one deployable. A **modular monolith** is one deployable with strict internal module boundaries. **Microservices** are independently deployable services that own their data and communicate over the network.

## Why monoliths are fine
One codebase, one deploy, in-process calls (fast and transactional), simple local development and debugging. Most products should start here. The usual failure is not the monolith but a **big ball of mud** with no boundaries.

## The modular monolith
Divide by **business capability** (orders, billing, catalog), not by technical layer. Each module exposes a small public API, hides its tables, and talks to others through that API or events, never by reaching into another module's database tables. This keeps a later split cheap.

## What microservices cost
Network failure and latency on every call, distributed transactions (no ACID across services), eventual consistency, schema and API versioning, deployment and observability overhead (tracing, per-service dashboards), and a team structure that must match. They pay off for independent scaling, independent release cadence for large teams, fault isolation, or different tech needs.

## Boundaries: domain-driven design lite
A **bounded context** is where a model and its language are consistent ("customer" in billing differs from "customer" in support). Align service or module boundaries to bounded contexts. If two services always change together or call each other constantly, the boundary is wrong.

## Migrating
**Strangler fig**: route one capability at a time to a new service behind the same entry point, until the old code is gone. Avoid a big-bang rewrite.

## Data ownership
Each service owns its data; others ask through an API or subscribe to events. A shared database across services is a hidden monolith. Use the **outbox pattern** to publish events reliably and **sagas** for multi-step business transactions with compensations.

lessons.title: API styles and patterns
lessons.summary: REST, GraphQL, gRPC and tRPC, plus BFF, versioning, pagination and idempotency.
lessons.body:
## Choosing a style
- **REST/HTTP JSON**: resources and verbs, cacheable, universally understood. Best default for public APIs.
- **GraphQL**: the client asks for exactly the fields it needs through one endpoint. Great for many different clients and nested data; costs: caching is harder, **N+1 resolver queries** (solve with batching such as DataLoader), query cost/depth limits needed for safety.
- **gRPC**: binary Protobuf over HTTP/2, strongly typed contracts, streaming. Best for **internal service-to-service** calls.
- **tRPC / server functions**: end-to-end TypeScript types when client and server live in one repo (and Next.js Server Actions).
- **WebSockets / SSE**: server push. SSE is simpler for one-way streams; WebSockets for two-way.

## Backend for frontend (BFF)
A thin server per client type (web, mobile) that aggregates downstream calls and shapes responses for that UI. It cuts chattiness and keeps client logic small.

## Design details that interviews probe
- **Versioning**: avoid breaking changes; add fields, deprecate gradually, version in the URL or a header when you must.
- **Pagination**: cursor-based for large or changing data; always cap page size.
- **Filtering and sorting**: whitelist fields; index what you allow.
- **Idempotency**: `Idempotency-Key` for unsafe operations; safe retries with exponential backoff and jitter on the client.
- **Errors**: consistent JSON, correct status codes (400 validation, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404, 409 conflict, 429 rate limited, 5xx server).
- **Rate limiting**: per user or key with token bucket; return `Retry-After`.
- **Caching**: `ETag` and `Cache-Control` with conditional requests (`If-None-Match` returns 304).
- **Auth**: OAuth 2.0 / OIDC for delegated access, short-lived access tokens, scopes.
- **Webhooks**: sign payloads (HMAC), retry with backoff, deliver at least once, and let receivers deduplicate by event id.

## Contracts
Describe APIs with OpenAPI (REST) or schemas (GraphQL, Protobuf), generate clients and types, and test contracts in CI so changes don't silently break consumers.

lessons.title: Caching, queues and reliable messaging
lessons.summary: Cache-aside, invalidation, stampedes, queues, the outbox pattern and sagas.
lessons.body:
## Caching patterns
- **Cache-aside**: read the cache; on a miss, load from the database and populate. Writes update the database then **invalidate** (delete) the key. The default pattern.
- **Write-through**: write to cache and database together. Simple reads, slower writes.
- **Write-behind**: write to cache and flush asynchronously. Fast but risks loss.
- **TTL** bounds staleness; choose it from how wrong the data may be.

## The hard parts
- **Invalidation**: the real problem. Prefer short TTLs plus explicit deletes on writes, and keys that include a version.
- **Stampede (thundering herd)**: a hot key expires and thousands of requests hit the database. Mitigate with request coalescing (one loader per key), a lock, soft/early expiry with jitter, or serving stale while revalidating.
- **Hot keys and big values**: replicate or shard hot keys; keep values small.
- **Consistency**: a cache can lag the database; decide whether that is acceptable per use case.
- **Layers**: browser, CDN, application, database cache. Each layer needs its own invalidation story.

## Queues and streams
A queue decouples producers from consumers, absorbs spikes and lets slow work happen in the background. Delivery is usually **at least once**, so consumers must be **idempotent** (dedupe by message id). Use a **dead-letter queue** for poison messages, retries with backoff, and visibility timeouts. A log/stream (Kafka) keeps ordered, replayable events per partition; ordering is guaranteed only within a partition, so choose the key accordingly.

## The dual-write problem and the outbox
Writing to the database and publishing a message are two systems: one can succeed while the other fails. The **transactional outbox** writes the business row and an outbox row in the **same transaction**; a relay process reads the outbox and publishes, retrying until acknowledged. Consumers dedupe.

## Sagas
A business process across services (reserve stock, charge card, ship) becomes a sequence of local transactions with **compensating actions** on failure (release stock, refund). Coordinate by **choreography** (services react to events) or **orchestration** (a coordinator drives steps).

## Backpressure
Bound queues, limit consumer concurrency, and shed or slow producers rather than letting memory grow until the process dies.

lessons.title: Reliability and observability
lessons.summary: Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, SLOs, the three pillars and safe deployments.
lessons.body:
## Failure is normal
Networks drop packets, dependencies slow down, disks fill, deploys break things. Design so a failing dependency degrades the product instead of taking it down.

## The resilience toolkit
- **Timeouts** on every outbound call. No timeout means a slow dependency ties up all your threads or connections.
- **Retries** with **exponential backoff and jitter**, only for idempotent operations, with a retry budget. Naive retries multiply load on a struggling service (a retry storm).
- **Circuit breaker**: after repeated failures, stop calling for a while (open), then probe (half-open). Fail fast and use a fallback.
- **Bulkheads**: isolate pools so one dependency can't exhaust everything.
- **Rate limiting and load shedding**: protect the service; reject early with 429/503 instead of collapsing.
- **Graceful degradation**: serve cached or partial results.
- **Redundancy** across zones, health checks, and automatic failover; avoid single points of failure.

## SLIs, SLOs and error budgets
An **SLI** is a measured indicator (the fraction of requests under 300 ms and non-5xx). An **SLO** is the target (99.9% over 30 days). The **error budget** is the allowed failure (0.1%, about 43 minutes a month). If you are burning it, slow feature work and fix reliability.

## Observability: three pillars
- **Logs**: structured JSON events with a request id, no secrets.
- **Metrics**: numeric time series; track the **RED** method for services (Rate, Errors, Duration) and **USE** for resources (Utilisation, Saturation, Errors). Watch percentiles (p95/p99), not averages.
- **Traces**: follow one request across services (OpenTelemetry) to find where time goes.

Alert on **symptoms users feel** (error rate, latency SLO burn), not on every CPU spike, and attach a runbook.

## Safe deployments
Automated tests and CI, **canary** or **blue-green** releases, **feature flags** to decouple deploy from release, quick **rollback**, and database migrations that are backward compatible (expand and contract).

## After an incident
Blameless postmortem: timeline, contributing factors, what detection and mitigation worked, and concrete follow-ups with owners.

projects.title: Event-driven orders service
projects.summary: An order API that reserves stock, takes payment and ships, using the transactional outbox, idempotent consumers and a saga with compensations.
projects.why: It teaches the hardest practical part of backend work: keeping data consistent across steps and systems without distributed transactions. The patterns (outbox, idempotency, sagas, retries, DLQs) are the vocabulary of senior backend interviews.
projects.architecture:
```
POST /orders (Idempotency-Key) -> Orders module
   tx: insert order(status=PENDING) + outbox(OrderCreated)   <- same transaction
Outbox relay -> queue -> Inventory consumer: reserve stock -> emits StockReserved / StockFailed
                      -> Payments consumer: charge (idempotent by order id) -> PaymentSucceeded / PaymentFailed
Saga: on failure -> compensations (release stock, cancel order)
```
Key decisions: choreography vs an orchestrator, an `order_status` state machine with allowed transitions, dedupe table per consumer.

projects.title: Payments ledger on CockroachDB
projects.summary: A double-entry ledger with idempotent transfers, serializable transactions with retries, and a multi-region design write-up.
projects.why: A ledger has strict correctness needs (no lost or double-spent money), which is exactly where a serializable distributed SQL database shines and where you must handle retries and contention properly. It shows depth with a distributed database, not just another Postgres CRUD app.
projects.architecture:
```
POST /transfers (Idempotency-Key)
  -> BEGIN (serializable)
       insert transfer(id=idempotency key) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
       insert 2 entries: debit(account A), credit(account B)
       update balances (or derive from entries)
     COMMIT   <- retry the whole block on SQLSTATE 40001
GET /accounts/:id/statement -> entries ordered by time, cursor paginated
```
Key decisions: money as integer minor units, an append-only `entries` table, UUID primary keys (no hot range), balances either derived or maintained with care for contention.

projects.title: Collaborative notes (realtime) with Next.js
projects.summary: Notes that several people edit at once with live cursors and conflict-free merging, plus offline support and version history.
projects.why: Collaborative editing is the textbook example of hard distributed state. Using a CRDT library teaches you convergence, ordering and persistence without hand-rolling operational transforms, and it is a memorable project to discuss.
projects.architecture:
```
Editor (Yjs doc) <-WebSocket provider-> Sync server (Node) <-> persistence (update log + snapshots)
Next.js app: auth, document list, sharing/permissions, history UI
```
Key decisions: CRDT (Yjs) so concurrent edits merge without a central lock, an append-only update log with periodic snapshots, permissions checked on every connection, awareness data (cursors) kept ephemeral.
